query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid framework that replaces explicit ab initio molecular dynamics with a machine‐learning–based interatomic potential (e.g., a moment tensor potential) combined with a perturbative thermodynamic integration correction can faithfully reproduce the free energies (including vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions) of solid and fluid states at fusion conditions while substantially reducing computational cost.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental and binary metals (e.g., pure Ni or Ni–Co alloys) previously validated, extended to multicomponent high-entropy alloys in their high-temperature, disordered or paramagnetic solid and corresponding fluid states.
generation.intervention: Develop and train an ML interatomic potential on a strategically selected subset of ab initio data that includes snapshots with key anharmonic distortions and electron-vibration features. Then, apply a thermodynamic integration (or free energy perturbation) scheme using this ML model to compute free energies across both solid and fluid phases, including post-hoc perturbative corrections to better capture entropic contributions.
generation.conditions: Temperature range approximately 1000–3000 K where vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration couplings are significant; compositions starting from validated elemental and binary systems extending to multicomponent alloys with moderate chemical order.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic environments and short-range ordering in disordered high-temperature phases, which are adequately captured in the ML training set.
generation.mechanism: The ML model reduces the computational demand by quickly approximating the high-dimensional free energy landscape, while the thermodynamic integration step recovers detailed entropy contributions (vibrational, anharmonic, electronic). This combined approach leverages past successes of ML potentials in reproducing DFT energies and forces, and integrates corrections based on perturbative methods to maintain fidelity to expensive ab initio methods.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion free energies and phase-transition observables will be predicted with accuracy comparable to explicit ab initio MD (errors near or below 5–10 meV/atom), but at computational speeds that are 10–100 times faster than DFT-based MD and competitive or superior to TOR-TILD when moving to multicomponent systems.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics calculations and TOR-TILD evaluations on elemental and binary systems serving as reference points.
generation.boundary: Validated for systems where the underlying potential energy landscape is not dominated by extreme configurational or magnetic order (e.g., high-temperature disordered phases, FCC/BCC) and for alloys with up to five or more elements. Outside of these composition or temperature regimes (e.g., significantly below 1000 K with strong ordering) the method’s error bounds may increase.
generation.uncertainty: The accurate incorporation of electron–vibration coupling and full anharmonic effects within the ML framework is not fully established; further tuning may be required especially for extremely multicomponent high-entropy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Implement the hybrid ML potential plus thermodynamic integration method on a well-characterized elemental system (e.g., pure Ni) and a binary alloy (e.g., Ni–Co) for which ab initio MD and TOR-TILD benchmarks exist. Calculate complete free energy curves for both solid and fluid phases over the 1000–3000 K range and compare the fusion free energies and derived observables (e.g., phase-transition temperature, vibrational entropy) against the benchmark data.
measurements: Total free energy (in meV/atom) of solid and fluid phases
Decomposed contributions from vibrational and electronic entropies
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the free energy differences or phase-transition observables deviate from the ab initio MD or TOR-TILD benchmarks by more than about 10% (or exceed an error of ~10 meV/atom), or if the computational speedup is less than an order of magnitude relative to the ab initio MD workflow, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It was found that the formation energy of hcp CrCoNi at 0 K is slightly lower than that of fcc CrCoNi, which implies that the hcp structure can be a competing phase during the synthesis of CrCoNi (Supplementary Fig. 1). The energy difference at 0 K between fcc and hcp CrCoNi was found to be ∼7 meV per atom (that is, 0.68 kJ mol−1). According to our free-energy calculations based on the quasi-harmonic approximation (Supplementary Fig. 2), the fcc structure gains a free-energy advantage at higher temperatures (for example, 500 K), due mainly to the contribution from lattice vibration. Similar results (namely that hcp is stable at low temperatures and fcc at higher temperatures) were obtained recently for the 5-element HEA, CrMnFeCoNi, when, in addition to configurational entropy, other entropic contributions including electronic, vibrational and magnetic were included in the total energy calculations. Lattice distortions arising from size mismatches of the constituent atoms in the CrCoNi MEA with the fcc or hcp structure were also examined from the atomic pair-distribution functions (PDFs) of CrCoNi crystals; these PDFs of fcc and hcp CrCoNi at 0 K are shown in Supplementary Fig. 3.

In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems,. Here, using training data reported previously for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost. The flowchart for constructing the MTP is shown in Fig. 1a with the methodological details provided in “Methods”. The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Figure 1b, c shows a comparison of the DFT- and MTP-predicted energies and forces for both training and test sets.
